To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a simple computational model, based on empirically measured parameters of neurogenesis, can recapitulate the basic landscape of mammalian cortex development.

(i) the number of neurons across the mammalian cortex is a function of the rate of progenitor cell division and death and of the ratio of terminal versus proliferative divisions, and (ii) the spatiotemporally varying kinetics of these processes can account for the spatially graded variations in the number of mature neurons in the cerebral cortices of different species.
a simple model of neurogenesis can explain the great diversity of the mammalian cerebral cortex in terms of the basic mechanisms that generate it.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the genome molds the developing cortex, and how the dynamics of cortical neurogenesis vary across the cortex and across species.
how the cerebral cortex, which has evolved to support the most complex cognitive functions, has achieved this by increasing in size and complexity.
understanding how the genome can sculpt the cerebral cortex, a key feature of the human brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the diversity of the cerebral cortex is the result of a conserved process, and that the diversity in the mature architecture of the cortex is a direct product of the dynamics of neurogenic development.

the basic process of cortical neurogenesis has been conserved across species, but its dynamics have been modulated to produce the great diversity in cortical neuron number and cortical architecture across mammals.
the basic process which populates cortical neurons is conserved and invariant across mammals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the mammalian brain, the number of cortical cells is a consequence of the dynamics of neurogenic cell division, and that these dynamics are subject to evolutionary selection.

the great diversity in cortical neuron number and the graded variations in cortical architecture across species and across a given cortex can be explained as arising from a conserved, fundamental process which populating the cortex with neurons.

the diversity in cerebral cortical structure across species and across spatial axes within species is not the result of special evolutionary mechanisms but rather the necessary consequence of a conserved, fundamental process of cortical neurogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

these features of the cortex are not the result of special evolutionary adaptations, but rather are the natural product of a conscripted developmental process, the kinetics of which vary across species and within a single cortex.

a conserved mechanism of cortical neurogenesis, with subtle changes in its kinetics, is sufficient to generate the great diversity in cortical size, and in the number and spatial arrangement of neurons, that is seen across mammalian species.
the diversity in the size of the mature cortex, and in its spatial organization, arises from a conserved mechanism, which can be understood by modeling the dynamics of neurogenetic processes.
